title: Element 12: Construction Activities
learningObjectives: Identify the principal hazards specific to construction activities
Explain how CDM regulations assign duties across the project team
Describe safe practices for demolition, lifting, and groundwork
Apply knowledge of construction safety to Gulf project requirements

content.text: Construction consistently has one of the highest fatality rates of any industry. The 'fatal four' — falls from height, struck by, electrocution, and caught in/between — account for the majority of construction deaths globally.

rows: Falls from scaffolding, roofs, ladders, MEWP; falling objects striking workers below
Excavation collapse, buried services, unstable ground
Lifting operations, crane collapse, vehicle-pedestrian conflict
Underground electrical, gas, water; overhead power lines
Noise, dust (silica), vibration, extremes of weather, UV
Cement (dermatitis, chemical burns), asbestos, solvents, diesel fumes
Manual handling, repetitive work, working in confined spaces

content.text: CDM Regulations (UK and internationally adopted) place legal duties on all parties in the construction supply chain, not just contractors. The principle is that hazards should be designed out during project planning, before construction starts.

rows: Appoint CDM Coordinator/Principal Designer and Principal Contractor; allow adequate time and resources; notify regulator for notifiable projects
Eliminate foreseeable hazards at design stage; provide information on remaining hazards; provide health and safety file
Plan, manage and coordinate construction phase; produce Construction Phase Plan; ensure welfare facilities provided
Plan and manage own work safely; provide information to workers; cooperate with Principal Contractor
Follow site rules; use equipment correctly; cooperate with managers; report hazards

content.text: CDM's key principle: hazards eliminated at design stage cost nothing. Hazards controlled during construction cost time and money. Hazards that cause accidents cost lives and far more money. Design out the risk early.
Lifting operations and lifting equipment (LOLER/equivalent standards) are among the most controlled activities in construction and O&G. Crane and lifting failures cause multiple fatalities.

items: Competency — Appointed persons, crane operators, and riggers must all be trained and certificated
Lift plan — Every non-routine or complex lift requires a written lift plan; includes ground-bearing capacity
Radius and capacity — Never exceed safe working load (SWL) for the radius; refer to crane load charts
Pre-use inspection — Every day before use; thorough examination by competent person every 6 months
Exclusion zone — Clear area under and around the load; banksman maintains communications
Slings and lifting gear — Colour-coded annual inspection tags; discard damaged slings; correct angle factor

content.text: Gulf mega-projects routinely involve extremely heavy lifts — modular construction in Qatar's LNG expansion required lifts over 2,000 tonnes. Aramco requires a Lifting Coordinator to be present on all lifts over 10 tonnes. Crane operators must hold Aramco-recognised certification. All lifting equipment must have valid Saudi Aramco or ADNOC-approved inspection certification.
Demolition is statistically the most dangerous construction activity. Planning must begin before work starts.

items: Pre-demolition survey — Structural survey; services identification; asbestos/hazardous material survey
Asbestos — Must be removed by licensed contractors before any demolition proceeds
Structural stability — Demolish in planned sequence; temporary propping; avoid creating unstable structures
Methods — Soft strip (internal fit-out), mechanical demolition (excavators), explosives (specialist only)
Exclusion zones — Adequate distance from falling structure; dust suppression

content.text: A naturally occurring fibrous mineral. Three main types: chrysotile (white), amosite (brown), crocidolite (blue — most dangerous). Inhaling asbestos fibres causes asbestosis, mesothelioma (always fatal), and lung cancer. There is no safe level of exposure. Banned in many countries but still present in buildings constructed before 1999.

Never cut, drill, or disturb suspected asbestos-containing material (ACM) without first having it tested and without appointing licensed removal contractors. Asbestos fibre release is invisible to the naked eye. Mesothelioma has a latency period of 20–50 years — workers may not know they were exposed until decades later.

Older industrial facilities in Gulf countries — particularly those built in the 1970s and 1980s during the first oil boom — may contain asbestos in insulation, ceiling tiles, gaskets, and pipe lagging. Renovation or demolition of these facilities requires asbestos surveys (HSG264 equivalent) before work starts. GCC countries have increasingly adopted strict asbestos regulations aligned with international standards.
